claim: Escherichia coli (E. coli) proliferates in the intestinal lumen of Caenorhabditis elegans during aging.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, Escherichia coli, which is its bacterial diet, proliferates in its intestinal lumen during aging.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing increased CFU over time.

claim: Progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli activates the transcription factor DAF-16 in C. elegans.
source: Here, we demonstrate that progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli activates the transcription factor DAF-16, which is required for maintenance of longevity and organismal fitness in worms with age.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing DAF-16::GFP nuclear translocation in worms fed live E. coli over time (Figure 1A, B).

claim: DAF-16 is required for maintenance of longevity and organismal fitness in worms with age.
source: Here, we demonstrate that progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli activates the transcription factor DAF-16, which is required for maintenance of longevity and organismal fitness in worms with age.
evidence: Supported by lifespan assays showing daf-16 mutants have shortened lifespan when fed live E. coli (Figure 1D).

claim: DAF-16 up-regulates two lysozymes lys-7 and lys-8 to limit bacterial accumulation in the gut during aging.
source: DAF-16 up-regulates two lysozymes lys-7 and lys-8, thus limiting the bacterial accumulation in the gut of worms during aging.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression analysis showing lys-7 and lys-8 are up-regulated in a DAF-16-dependent manner (Figure 7).

claim: The levels of indole produced by E. coli are increased in worms during dysbiosis.
source: During dysbiosis, the levels of indole produced by E. coli are increased in worms.
evidence: Measured directly showing indole levels of 30.9, 71.9, and 105.9 nmol/g dry weight on days 1, 4, and 7 respectively (Figure 2C).

claim: Indole is involved in the activation of DAF-16 by TRPA-1 in neurons of worms.
source: Indole is involved in the activation of DAF-16 by TRPA-1 in neurons of worms.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 suppresses indole-mediated DAF-16 activation (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Indole functions as a microbial signal of gut dysbiosis to promote fitness of the host.
source: Our finding demonstrates that indole functions as a microbial signal of gut dysbiosis to promote fitness of the host.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing indole extends lifespan and reduces bacterial accumulation in a DAF-16-dependent manner.

claim: The nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine was increased in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7.
source: The nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine was increased in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7, but not in age-matched WT worms fed heat-killed (HK) E. coli OP50 (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy images showing percentage of worms with nuclear DAF-16::GFP (Figure 1A, B).

claim: DAF-16 was retained in the cytoplasm of the intestine in worms fed heat-killed E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7.
source: The nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine was increased in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7, but not in age-matched WT worms fed heat-killed (HK) E. coli OP50 (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Shown by quantification of DAF-16 localization in Figure 1B.

claim: The expression of dod-3p::gfp was significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on day 4.
source: As expected, the expression of either dod-3p::gfp or hsp-16.2p::nCherry was significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on day 4, but not in age-matched worms fed HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Measured by fluorescence intensity quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The expression of hsp-16.2p::nCherry was significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on day 4.
source: As expected, the expression of either dod-3p::gfp or hsp-16.2p::nCherry was significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on day 4, but not in age-matched worms fed HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Measured by fluorescence intensity quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: DAF-16 was also retained in the cytoplasm of the intestine in worms fed ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7.
source: Likewise, DAF-16 was also retained in the cytoplasm of the intestine in worms fed ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1C showing cytoplasmic localization.

claim: Starvation induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine of worms on day 1.
source: In contrast, starvation induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine of worms on day 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Either heat-killed or antibiotic-killed E. coli OP50 as a food source does not induce a starvation state in worms.
source: Thus, either HK or antibiotic-killed E. coli OP50 as a food source does not induce a starvation state in worms.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of DAF-16 localization patterns between killed bacteria and starvation conditions.

claim: The activation of DAF-16 is mainly attributed to the presence of live E. coli, but not by age itself, in worms.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the activation of DAF-16 is mainly attributed to the presence of live E. coli, but not by age itself, in worms.
evidence: Concluded from experiments comparing live vs. killed bacteria across different ages.

claim: daf-16(mu86) mutants grown on live E. coli OP50 had a shorter lifespan than those grown on HK E. coli OP50.
source: Consistent with the previous observations (Li et al., 2019; Portal-Celhay et al., 2012), we found that a mutation in daf-16(mu86) shortened the lifespan of worms fed live E. coli OP50 at 20°C (Figure 1D). In contrast, the mutation in daf-16(mu86) had no impact on the lifespan of worms fed either HK (Figure 1D) or ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by lifespan curves in Figure 1D showing significant difference.

claim: The mutation in daf-16(mu86) had no impact on the lifespan of worms fed heat-killed E. coli OP50.
source: In contrast, the mutation in daf-16(mu86) had no impact on the lifespan of worms fed either HK (Figure 1D) or ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 1D.

claim: The mutation in daf-16(mu86) had no impact on the lifespan of worms fed ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50.
source: In contrast, the mutation in daf-16(mu86) had no impact on the lifespan of worms fed either HK (Figure 1D) or ampicillin-killed E. coli OP50 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 1E.

claim: The rates of pharyngeal pumping were reduced in daf-16(mu86) mutants on day 7 compared to WT worms fed live E. coli OP50.
source: Both the rates of pharyngeal pumping (Figure 1F) and body bending (Figure 1G) were reduced in daf-16(mu86) mutants on day 7 as compared to those in WT worms fed live E. coli OP50.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1F showing significant reduction.

claim: The rates of body bending were reduced in daf-16(mu86) mutants on day 7 compared to WT worms fed live E. coli OP50.
source: Both the rates of pharyngeal pumping (Figure 1F) and body bending (Figure 1G) were reduced in daf-16(mu86) mutants on day 7 as compared to those in WT worms fed live E. coli OP50.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1G showing significant reduction.

claim: The rates of pharyngeal pumping and body bending were comparable in WT worms and daf-16(mu86) mutants grown on HK E. coli OP50 on day 7.
source: In contrast, the rates of pharyngeal pumping and body bending were comparable in WT worms and daf-16(mu86) mutants grown on HK E. coli OP50 on day 7.
evidence: Stated as no significant difference in the text, supported by data in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The body-cavity leakage in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 7 and 10 were higher than those in age-matched WT worms fed live E. coli OP50.
source: Furthermore, we used food dye FD&C Blue No. 1 to evaluate the integrity of intestinal barrier (Ma et al., 2020). The body-cavity leakage in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 7 and 10 were higher than those in age-matched WT worms fed live E. coli OP50, but not HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1I showing significant increase in leakage.

claim: The body-cavity leakage in daf-16(mu86) mutants was not different from WT worms when fed HK E. coli OP50.
source: The body-cavity leakage in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 7 and 10 were higher than those in age-matched WT worms fed live E. coli OP50, but not HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 1I.

claim: The activation of DAF-16 by bacterial accumulation is required for normal lifespan and the maintenance of organismal fitness.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the activation of DAF-16 by bacterial accumulation is required for normal lifespan and the maintenance of organismal fitness.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing effects on lifespan and fitness markers.

claim: A candidate compound from E. coli OP50 culture supernatants was identified as indole with mass spectrometry and NMR data.
source: A candidate compound was detected by activity-guided isolation, and further identified as indole with mass spectrometry and NMR data (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Structural identification confirmed by MS and NMR spectra shown in figures.

claim: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) significantly induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16.
source: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) not only significantly induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 (Figure 2B), but also up-regulated the expression of either dod-3p::gfp or hsp-16.2p::nCherry in young adult worms after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2B showing dose-dependent nuclear localization.

claim: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) up-regulated the expression of dod-3p::gfp in young adult worms after 24 hr of treatment.
source: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) not only significantly induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 (Figure 2B), but also up-regulated the expression of either dod-3p::gfp or hsp-16.2p::nCherry in young adult worms after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) up-regulated the expression of hsp-16.2p::nCherry in young adult worms after 24 hr of treatment.
source: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) not only significantly induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 (Figure 2B), but also up-regulated the expression of either dod-3p::gfp or hsp-16.2p::nCherry in young adult worms after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The levels of indole were 30.9, 71.9, and 105.9 nmol/g dry weight, respectively, in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 1, 4, and 7.
source: Next, we found that the levels of indole were 30.9, 71.9, and 105.9 nmol/g dry weight, respectively, in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 1, 4, and 7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The elevated indole levels in worms were accompanied by an increase in colony-forming units (CFU) of live E. coli OP50 in the intestine of worms with age.
source: The elevated indole levels in worms were accompanied by an increase in colony-forming units (CFU) of live E. coli OP50 in the intestine of worms with age (Figure 2C), suggesting that accumulation of live E. coli OP50 in the intestine is probably responsible for increased indole in worms.
evidence: Shown by parallel measurements of CFU and indole levels in Figure 2C.

claim: The levels of indole were 28.2, 31.6, and 36.1 nmol/g dry weight, respectively, in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 on days 1, 4, and 7.
source: However, we found that the levels of indole were 28.2, 31.6, and 36.1 nmol/g dry weight, respectively, in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 on days 1, 4, and 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that indole was not accumulated in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 even for 7 days.
evidence: Measured by LC-MS shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Indole was not accumulated in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 even for 7 days.
source: However, we found that the levels of indole were 28.2, 31.6, and 36.1 nmol/g dry weight, respectively, in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 on days 1, 4, and 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that indole was not accumulated in worms fed HK E. coli OP50 even for 7 days.
evidence: Concluded from stable indole levels over time in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The increase in the levels of indole in worms results from intestinal accumulation of live E. coli OP50, rather than exogenous indole produced by E. coli OP50 on the NGM plates.
source: Thus, the increase in the levels of indole in worms results from intestinal accumulation of live E. coli OP50, rather than exogenous indole produced by E. coli OP50 on the NGM plates.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of indole levels in worms fed live vs. killed bacteria.

claim: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) significantly increased the indole levels in young adult worms on day 1.
source: Supplementation with indole (50–200 μM) significantly increased the indole levels in young adult worms on day 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which could induce nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms (Figure 2B).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In bacteria, indole is biosynthesized from tryptophan by tryptophanase (tnaA).
source: In bacteria, indole is biosynthesized from tryptophan by tryptophanase (tnaA) (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from established literature (Lee et al., 2015).

claim: Both tnaA mRNA and indole levels were undetectable in the K-12 ΔtnaA strain.
source: We found that both tnaA mRNA and indole levels were undetectable in the K-12 ΔtnaA strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: Measured by qPCR and LC-MS in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Disruption of tnaA significantly suppressed the nuclear translocation of DAF-16.
source: Furthermore, disruption of tnaA significantly suppressed the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2D showing reduced nuclear localization.

claim: DAF-16::GFP was mainly located in the cytoplasm of the intestine in worms fed live K-12 ΔtnaA strains on day 4.
source: The nuclear translocation of DAF-16::GFP was mainly located in the cytoplasm of the intestine in worms fed live K-12 ΔtnaA strains on day 4.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Supplementation with indole induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16::GFP in the intestine of worms fed K-12 ΔtnaA strains.
source: However, supplementation with indole induced the nuclear translocation of DAF-16::GFP in the intestine of these worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Shown by quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The production of indole in the K12ΔtnaA::tnaA strains bacterial solution was 34.1 μmol/l, similar to the K12 strains.
source: Moreover, we rescued the expression of tnaA in the K-12ΔtnaA strains, and found that the production of indole in the K12ΔtnaA::tnaA strains bacterial solution was 34.1 μmol/l, similar to the K12 strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: DAF-16::GFP was mainly located in the nuclear of the intestine in worms fed live K12ΔtnaA::tnaA strains on days 4 and 7.
source: DAF-16::GFP was mainly located in the nuclear of the intestine in worms fed live K12ΔtnaA::tnaA strains on days 4 and 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E showing nuclear localization.

claim: Indole is involved in the activation of DAF-16 in worms with age.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that indole is involved in the activation of DAF-16 in worms with age.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments with tnaA mutants and indole supplementation.

claim: Exogenous indole extends lifespan in C. elegans at 16°C.
source: It has been shown that exogenous indole extends lifespan in C. elegans at 16°C (Sonowal et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Sonowal et al., 2017).

claim: Adult worms fed E. coli K-12 tnaA strains exhibited a shortened lifespan at 20°C, compared with those fed E. coli K-12 strain.
source: We found that adult worms fed E. coli K-12 tnaA strains exhibited a shortened lifespan at 20°C, compared with those fed E. coli K-12 strain (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 3A.

claim: Supplementation with indole in adults rescued the shortened lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain.
source: Supplementation with indole in adults not only rescued the shortened lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain, but also significantly extended the lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 strain (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 3A.

claim: Supplementation with indole significantly extended the lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 strain.
source: Supplementation with indole in adults not only rescued the shortened lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain, but also significantly extended the lifespan of WT worms fed E. coli K-12 strain (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 3A.

claim: The lifespan of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain was comparable to that of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed E. coli K-12 strain.
source: In contrast, the lifespan of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain was comparable to that of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed E. coli K-12 strain (Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 3B.

claim: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) did not affect the lifespan of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed either E. coli K-12 or K-12 tnaA strain.
source: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) did not affect the lifespan of daf-16(mu86) mutants fed either E. coli K-12 or K-12 tnaA strain (Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 3B.

claim: The CFU of E. coli K-12 ΔnaA strain were significantly higher than those of E. coli K12 strain in WT worms on days 4 and 7.
source: Moreover, the CFU of E. coli K-12 ΔnaA strain were significantly higher than those of E. coli K12 strain in WT worms on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 3C.

claim: The CFU of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain were similar to those of E. coli K12 strain in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 4 and 7.
source: In contrast, the CFU of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain were similar to those of E. coli K12 strain in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 3D.

claim: The accumulation of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain expressing mCherry was significantly higher than that of E. coli K12 strain in WT worms on days 4 and 7.
source: Likewise, the accumulation of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain expressing mCherry was significantly higher than that of E. coli K12 strain in WT worms, but not daf-16(mu86) mutants, on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 3F.

claim: The accumulation of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain expressing mCherry was not different from E. coli K12 strain in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 4 and 7.
source: Likewise, the accumulation of E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain expressing mCherry was significantly higher than that of E. coli K12 strain in WT worms, but not daf-16(mu86) mutants, on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 3G.

claim: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) inhibited the CFU of E. coli K-12 in WT worms on days 4 and 7.
source: Finally, supplementation with indole (100 μM) inhibited the CFU of E. coli K-12 in WT worms, but not daf-16(mu86) mutants, on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 3H.

claim: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) did not inhibit the CFU of E. coli K-12 in daf-16(mu86) mutants on days 4 and 7.
source: Finally, supplementation with indole (100 μM) inhibited the CFU of E. coli K-12 in WT worms, but not daf-16(mu86) mutants, on days 4 and 7 (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 3I.

claim: Indole produced by bacteria in the gut inhibits the proliferation of E. coli through DAF-16, thereby maintaining normal lifespan in worms.
source: These results suggest that indole produced by bacteria in the gut inhibits the proliferation of E. coli through DAF-16, thereby maintaining normal lifespan in worms.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing indole effects on CFU and lifespan depend on DAF-16.

claim: C. elegans xenobiotic receptor AHR-1 encodes an ortholog of the mammalian AHR.
source: Previously, Sonowal et al. have identified that C. elegans xenobiotic receptor AHR-1, which encodes an ortholog of the mammalian AHR, mediates indole-promoted lifespan extension in worms at 16°C (Sonowal et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Sonowal et al., 2017).

claim: RNAi knockdown of ahr-1 did not affect the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on day 7.
source: However, we found that RNAi knockdown of ahr-1 did not affect the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi knockdown of ahr-1 did not affect the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr.
source: However, we found that RNAi knockdown of ahr-1 did not affect the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bacteria-derived indole activates the transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA-1) in enteroendocrine cells in zebrafish and mammals.
source: A recent study has demonstrated that bacteria-derived indole activates the transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA-1), a cold-sensitive TRP channel, in enteroendocrine cells in zebrafish and mammals (Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from recent study (Ye et al., 2021).

claim: C. elegans TRPA-1 is an ortholog of mammalian TRPA-1.
source: As C. elegans TRPA-1 is an ortholog of mammalian TRPA-1 (Kindt et al., 2007; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007), we tested the role of TRPA-1 in DAF-16 activation by indole.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Kindt et al., 2007; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007).

claim: RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on days 4 and 7.
source: We found that RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on days 4 and 7 (Figure 4A) or young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4A showing reduced nuclear localization.

claim: RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr.
source: We found that RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in worms fed E. coli K12 strain on days 4 and 7 (Figure 4A) or young adult worms treated with indole (100 μM) for 24 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4B showing reduced nuclear localization.

claim: TRPA-1 is involved in indole-mediated DAF-16 activation.
source: These results suggest that TRPA-1 is involved in indole-mediated DAF-16 activation.
evidence: Concluded from RNAi experiments showing TRPA-1 is required for indole effects.

claim: TRPA-1 activated by low temperatures mediates calcium influx, which in turn stimulates the PKC-2-SGK-1 signaling to promote the transcription activity of DAF-16, leading to lifespan extension in worms.
source: Previously, Xiao et al., 2013 have demonstrated that TRPA-1 activated by low temperatures mediates calcium influx, which in turn stimulates the PKC-2-SGK-1 signaling to promote the transcription activity of DAF-16, leading to lifespan extension in worms.
evidence: Cited from previous study (Xiao et al., 2013).

claim: RNAi knockdown of sgk-1 did not influence the nuclear-cytoplasmic distribution of DAF-16 in the presence of indole.
source: However, we found that RNAi knockdown of sgk-1 did not influence the nuclear-cytoplasmic distribution of DAF-16 in the presence of indole (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mutant worms lacking trpa-1 exhibited a shorter lifespan than did WT worms at 20°C.
source: Mutant worms lacking trpa-1 exhibited a shorter lifespan than did WT worms at 20°C (Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Xiao et al., 2013).

claim: Knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi significantly shortened the lifespan of worms fed E. coli K12 strain.
source: Consistent with this observation, knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi significantly shortened the lifespan of worms fed E. coli K12 strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 4C.

claim: Supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of worms after knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi.
source: Supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of worms after knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi or in trpa-1(ok999) mutants (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 4C.

claim: Supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of trpa-1(ok999) mutants.
source: Supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of worms after knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi or in trpa-1(ok999) mutants (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In trpa-1(ok999) mutants, knockdown of daf-16 by RNAi did not further reduce the lifespan of worms.
source: In trpa-1(ok999) mutants, knockdown of daf-16 by RNAi did not further reduce the lifespan of worms (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The CFU of E. coli K-12 strain were significantly increased in worms subjected to trpa-1 RNAi on days 4 and 7.
source: Furthermore, the CFU of E. coli K-12 strain were significantly increased in worms subjected to trpa-1 RNAi on days 4 and 7 (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Supplementation with indole failed to suppress the increases in CFU in worms subjected to trpa-1 RNAi.
source: Supplementation with indole failed to suppress the increases in CFU in these worms.
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Supplementation with indole failed to suppress the increases in E. coli K-12 strain expressing mCherry in trpa-1(ok999) mutants subjected to empty vector or daf-16 RNAi.
source: In addition, supplementation with indole also failed to suppress the increases in E. coli K-12 strain expressing mCherry in trpa-1(ok999) mutants subjected to empty vector or daf-16 RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Indole exhibits its function in extending the lifespan and inhibiting bacterial accumulation primarily via TRPA-1.
source: These results suggest that indole exhibits its function in extending the lifespan and inhibiting bacterial accumulation primarily via TRPA-1.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing indole effects require TRPA-1.

claim: Podocarpic acid, a TRPA-1 agonist, activates the SEK-1/PMK-1/SKN-1 pathway.
source: It has been shown that podocarpic acid, a TRPA-1 agonist, activates the SEK-1/PMK-1/SKN-1 pathway (Chaudhuri et al., 2016), a signaling cascade involved in C. elegans defense against pathogenic bacteria (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Chaudhuri et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2002).

claim: Supplementation with 0.1 mM indole failed to induce nuclear localization of SKN-1::GFP in the intestine of transgenic worms.
source: However, we found that supplementation with 0.1 mM indole failed to induce nuclear localization of SKN-1::GFP in the intestine of the transgenic worms expressing skn-1p::skn-1::gfp (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B), suggesting that indole cannot activate SKN-1 in worms.
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Indole cannot activate SKN-1 in worms.
source: However, we found that supplementation with 0.1 mM indole failed to induce nuclear localization of SKN-1::GFP in the intestine of the transgenic worms expressing skn-1p::skn-1::gfp (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B), suggesting that indole cannot activate SKN-1 in worms.
evidence: Concluded from lack of SKN-1 nuclear localization with indole treatment.

claim: 0.02 mM of podocarpic acid did not induce the nuclear localization of DAF-16::GFP.
source: Furthermore, 0.02 mM of podocarpic acid did not induce the nuclear localization of DAF-16::GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: TRPA-1 activation via podocarpic acid and indole happens largely through distinct mechanisms.
source: These results suggest that TRPA-1 activation via podocarpic acid and indole happens largely through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on SKN-1 and DAF-16 activation.

claim: Overexpression of trpa-1 in both the intestine and neurons is sufficient to extend the lifespan of worms.
source: As overexpression of trpa-1 in both the intestine and neurons is sufficient to extend the lifespan of worms (Xiao et al., 2013), we determined tissue-specific activities of TRPA-1 in the regulation of longevity mediated by indole.
evidence: Cited from previous study (Xiao et al., 2013).

claim: Both neuronal- and intestinal-specific knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi significantly shortened the lifespan of worms.
source: Consistent with this observation (Xiao et al., 2013), we found that both neuronal- and intestinal-specific knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi significantly shortened the lifespan of worms (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) only extended the lifespan of worms subjected to intestinal specific trpa-1 RNAi.
source: However, supplementation with indole (100 μM) only extended the lifespan of worms subjected to intestinal specific (Figure 5B), but not neuronal specific, trpa-1 RNAi (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 5B.

claim: Supplementation with indole (100 μM) did not extend the lifespan of worms subjected to neuronal specific trpa-1 RNAi.
source: However, supplementation with indole (100 μM) only extended the lifespan of worms subjected to intestinal specific (Figure 5B), but not neuronal specific, trpa-1 RNAi (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of trpa-1 in either neurons or the intestine increased the CFU of E. coli K-12 in worms on days 4 and 7.
source: Likewise, knockdown of trpa-1 in either neurons (Figure 5C, D) or the intestine (Figure 5E, F) increased the CFU of E. coli K-12 in worms on days 4 and 7.
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 5C-F.

claim: Supplementation with indole failed to inhibit the increase in the CFU of E. coli K-12 in worms subjected to neuronal-specific trpa-1 RNAi.
source: However, supplementation with indole failed to inhibit the increase in the CFU of E. coli K-12 in worms subjected to neuronal-specific trpa-1 RNAi (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Supplementation with indole significantly suppressed the CFU of E. coli K-12 in worms subjected to intestinal-specific trpa-1 RNAi.
source: In contrast, supplementation with indole significantly suppressed the CFU of E. coli K-12 in these worms subjected to intestinal-specific trpa-1 RNAi (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 5E and F.

claim: TRPA-1 in neurons is involved in indole-mediated longevity.
source: These results suggest that TRPA-1 in neurons is involved in indole-mediated longevity.
evidence: Concluded from tissue-specific RNAi experiments showing neuronal TRPA-1 is required for indole effects.

claim: C. elegans possesses a variety of putative antimicrobial effector proteins, such as lysozymes, defensin-like peptides, neuropeptide-like proteins, and caenacins.
source: C. elegans possesses a variety of putative antimicrobial effector proteins, such as lysozymes, defensin-like peptides, neuropeptide-like proteins, and caenacins (Dierking et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Dierking et al., 2016).

claim: Lysozymes are involved in host defense against various pathogens.
source: Of these antimicrobial proteins, lysozymes are involved in host defense against various pathogens (Boehnisch et al., 2011; Irazoqui et al., 2010a; Mallo et al., 2002; O'Rourke et al., 2006; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Expressions of lysozyme genes, such as lys-2, lys-7, and lys-8, are markedly up-regulated in 4-day-old worms in a DAF-16-dependent manner.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that expressions of lysozyme genes, such as lys-2, lys-7, and lys-8, are markedly up-regulated in 4-day-old worms, which is dependent on DAF-16 (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Li et al., 2019).

claim: A single mutation in lys-7(ok1384) slightly but significantly reduced the lifespan of worms fed live E. coli OP50.
source: We found that a single mutation in lys-7(ok1384) slightly but significantly reduced the lifespan of worms fed live E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but not HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), which was consistent with a previous observation (Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A single mutation in lys-7(ok1384) did not affect the lifespan of worms fed HK E. coli OP50.
source: We found that a single mutation in lys-7(ok1384) slightly but significantly reduced the lifespan of worms fed live E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but not HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), which was consistent with a previous observation (Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A single mutation in lys-8(ok3504) did not affect the lifespan when worms were grown on live E. coli OP50.
source: In contrast, whereas either a single mutation in lys-8(ok3504) or RNAi knockdown of lys-2 did not affect the lifespan when worms were grown on live E. coli OP50, or HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi knockdown of lys-2 did not affect the lifespan when worms were grown on live E. coli OP50.
source: In contrast, whereas either a single mutation in lys-8(ok3504) or RNAi knockdown of lys-2 did not affect the lifespan when worms were grown on live E. coli OP50, or HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants exhibited a shortened lifespan when worms were fed live E. coli OP50.
source: However, lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants exhibited a shortened lifespan when worms were fed live E. coli OP50 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown by survival curves in Figure 6A.

claim: The lifespan of lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants was comparable to that of WT worms fed HK E. coli OP50.
source: In contrast, the lifespan of lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants was comparable to that of WT worms fed HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of lys-2 by RNAi did not affect the lifespan of lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants grown on live E. coli OP50.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of lys-2 by RNAi did not affect the lifespan of lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants grown on live E. coli OP50, or HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The rates of pharyngeal-pumping were reduced in 8-day-old lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants fed live E. coli OP50.
source: Both the rates of pharyngeal-pumping (Figure 6C) and body bending (Figure 6D) were reduced in 8-day-old lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants fed live E. coli OP50.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 6C showing significant reduction.

claim: The rates of body bending were reduced in 8-day-old lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants fed live E. coli OP50.
source: Both the rates of pharyngeal-pumping (Figure 6C) and body bending (Figure 6D) were reduced in 8-day-old lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants fed live E. coli OP50.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 6D showing significant reduction.

claim: The body-cavity leakage was increased in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants fed live E. coli OP50 on day 10.
source: Moreover, the body-cavity leakage was increased in the double mutants fed live E. coli OP50 on day 10 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 6E showing significant increase.

claim: Age-associated markers in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants were comparable to those in age-matched WT worms fed HK E. coli OP50.
source: However, these age-associated markers in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants were comparable to those in age-matched WT worms fed HK E. coli OP50.
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figures 6C-E.

claim: Double mutations in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) increased the CFU of E. coli OP50 in worms on day 7.
source: In addition, double mutations in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) increased the CFU of E. coli OP50 (Figure 6F) as well as the accumulation of E. coli OP50 expressing RFP in worms on day 7 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Quantified by CFU counting in Figure 6F.

claim: Double mutations in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) increased the accumulation of E. coli OP50 expressing RFP in worms on day 7.
source: In addition, double mutations in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) increased the CFU of E. coli OP50 (Figure 6F) as well as the accumulation of E. coli OP50 expressing RFP in worms on day 7 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 6G.

claim: Supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants.
source: Finally, we found that supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of worms and failed to suppress the increase the CFU of E. coli K-12 in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown by overlapping survival curves in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Supplementation with indole failed to suppress the increase in CFU of E. coli K-12 in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants.
source: Finally, we found that supplementation with indole no longer extended the lifespan of worms and failed to suppress the increase the CFU of E. coli K-12 in lys-7(ok1384); lys-8(ok3504) double mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp were significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7.
source: Using the transgenic worms expressing either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp, we found that the expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp were significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D), but not in age-matched worms fed HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: The expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp were not up-regulated in age-matched worms fed HK E. coli OP50.
source: Using the transgenic worms expressing either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp, we found that the expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp were significantly up-regulated in worms fed live E. coli OP50 on days 4 and 7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D), but not in age-matched worms fed HK E. coli OP50 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of daf-16 significantly suppressed the expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp in worms fed live E. coli OP50.
source: RNAi knockdown of daf-16 also significantly suppressed the expressions of lys-7p::gfp and lys-8p::gfp in these worms fed live E. coli OP50 (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 were reduced in daf-16(mu86) mutants.
source: Similar results were obtained by measuring the mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 in daf-16(mu86) mutants using quantitive real-time PCR (qPCR) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Measured by qPCR in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Expression of lys-7p::gfp was reduced in worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain on days 4 and 7, compared to those in age-matched worms fed E. coli K-12 strain.
source: Furthermore, we found that expression of either lys-7p::gfp (Figure 7C) or lys-8p::gfp (Figure 7D) was reduced in worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain on days 4 and 7, compared to those in age-matched worms fed E. coli K-12 strain.
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7C.

claim: Expression of lys-8p::gfp was reduced in worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain on days 4 and 7, compared to those in age-matched worms fed E. coli K-12 strain.
source: Furthermore, we found that expression of either lys-7p::gfp (Figure 7C) or lys-8p::gfp (Figure 7D) was reduced in worms fed E. coli K-12 ΔtnaA strain on days 4 and 7, compared to those in age-matched worms fed E. coli K-12 strain.
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7D.

claim: Indole (100 μM) remarkably increased the expression of lys-7p::gfp in young adult worms after 24 hr treatment.
source: Likewise, indole (100 μM) remarkably increased the expression of either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp in young adult worms after 24 hr treatment (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7E.

claim: Indole (100 μM) remarkably increased the expression of lys-8p::gfp in young adult worms after 24 hr treatment.
source: Likewise, indole (100 μM) remarkably increased the expression of either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp in young adult worms after 24 hr treatment (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7F.

claim: RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the expression of lys-7p::gfp in 4-day-old worms fed E. coli K12 strain.
source: Meanwhile, RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the expression of either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp in 4-day-old worms fed E. coli K12 strain (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7A.

claim: RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the expression of lys-8p::gfp in 4-day-old worms fed E. coli K12 strain.
source: Meanwhile, RNAi knockdown of trpa-1 significantly inhibited the expression of either lys-7p::gfp or lys-8p::gfp in 4-day-old worms fed E. coli K12 strain (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Quantified by fluorescence intensity in Figure 7B.

claim: The mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 were significantly down-regulated in worms subjected to neuronal specific knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi on day 4.
source: Finally, we found that the mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 were significantly down-regulated in worms subjected to neuronal specific (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), but not intestinal specific, knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi on day 4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Measured by qPCR in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 were not down-regulated in worms subjected to intestinal specific knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi on day 4.
source: Finally, we found that the mRNA levels of lys-7 and lys-8 were significantly down-regulated in worms subjected to neuronal specific (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), but not intestinal specific, knockdown of trpa-1 by RNAi on day 4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Supplementation with indole only up-regulated the expression of lys-7 and lys-8 in worms subjected to intestinal specific RNAi of trpa-1.
source: However, supplementation with indole only up-regulated the expression of lys-7 and lys-8 in worms subjected to intestinal specific (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C), but not neuronal specific, RNAi of trpa-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by qPCR in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Supplementation with indole did not up-regulate the expression of lys-7 and lys-8 in worms subjected to neuronal specific RNAi of trpa-1.
source: However, supplementation with indole only up-regulated the expression of lys-7 and lys-8 in worms subjected to intestinal specific (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C), but not neuronal specific, RNAi of trpa-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Shown by non-significant differences in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: LYS-7 and LYS-8 function as downstream molecules of DAF-16 to maintain normal lifespan by inhibiting bacterial proliferation in worms.
source: These results suggest that LYS-7 and LYS-8 function as downstream molecules of DAF-16 to maintain normal lifespan by inhibiting bacterial proliferation in worms.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing lys-7/lys-8 are regulated by DAF-16 and affect bacterial loads and lifespan.

claim: The intestinal lumen of worms is frequently distended during aging, which is accompanied by bacterial proliferation.
source: The intestinal lumen of worms is frequently distended during aging, which accompanied by bacterial proliferation (Garigan et al., 2002; McGee et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Garigan et al., 2002; McGee et al., 2011).

claim: Blockage of bacterial proliferation by treatment of UV, antibiotics, and heat extends lifespan of worms.
source: Blockage of bacterial proliferation by treatment of UV, antibiotics, and heat extends lifespan of worms (De Arras et al., 2014; Garigan et al., 2002; Hwang et al., 2014), implicating that progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli probably contributes to worm aging and death.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (De Arras et al., 2014; Garigan et al., 2002; Hwang et al., 2014).

claim: Progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli probably contributes to worm aging and death.
source: Blockage of bacterial proliferation by treatment of UV, antibiotics, and heat extends lifespan of worms (De Arras et al., 2014; Garigan et al., 2002; Hwang et al., 2014), implicating that progressive intestinal proliferation of E. coli probably contributes to worm aging and death.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking bacterial proliferation extends lifespan.

claim: Genetic inactivation of daf-16 accelerates tissue deterioration and shortens lifespan of wild-type worms grown on E. coli OP50.
source: Accumulating evidence has indicated that genetic inactivation of daf-16 accelerates tissue deterioration and shortens lifespan of wild-type (WT) worms grown on E. coli OP50 (Garigan et al., 2002; Li et al., 2019; Portal-Celhay and Blaser, 2012; Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies (Garigan et al., 2002; Li et al., 2019; Portal-Celhay and Blaser, 2012; Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).

claim: DAF-16 is activated during bacterial accumulation in older worms.
source: The observation that DAF-16 is activated during bacterial accumulation in older worms (Li et al., 2019) prompt us to investigate the role of DAF-16 in dysbiosis in the gut of worms.
evidence: Cited from previous study (Li et al., 2019).

claim: Indole is a well-known signaling molecule involved in regulation of a variety of physiological processes in bacteria.
source: As a well-known signaling molecule, indole is involved in regulation of a variety of physiological processes in bacteria, such as cell division, biofilm formation, virulence, spore formation, and antibiotic resistance (Lee et al., 2015; Zarkan et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Lee et al., 2015; Zarkan et al., 2020).

claim: Animals cannot synthesize indole, but they can sense and modify this metabolite.
source: Although animals cannot synthesize indole, they can sense and modify this metabolite (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Lee et al., 2015).

claim: Indole and its derivatives can influence insect behaviors and human diseases, such as intestinal inflammation and diabetes.
source: Indole and its derivatives can influence insect behaviors and human diseases, such as intestinal inflammation and diabetes (Agus et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Agus et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2015).

claim: Indole may function as an interspecies and interkingdom signaling molecule to influence the microbe–host interaction.
source: Thus, indole may function as an interspecies and interkingdom signaling molecule to influence the microbe–host interaction (Bansal et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Bansal et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2021).

claim: Enteric delivery of indole (1 mM) increases the intestinal motility by inducing 5-hydroxytryptamine secretion in zebrafish larvae.
source: For instance, enteric delivery of indole (1 mM) increases the intestinal motility by inducing 5-hydroxytryptamine secretion in zebrafish larvae (Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Ye et al., 2021).

claim: Supplementation with 0.2 mM indole enhances the resistance of C. elegans to infection with C. albicans by reducing fungal colonization in the intestine.
source: Supplementation with 0.2 mM indole enhances the resistance of C. elegans to infection with C. albicans by reducing fungal colonization in the intestine (Oh et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Oh et al., 2012).

claim: Treatment of HCT-8 intestinal epithelial cells with 1 mM indole inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) mediated activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and up-regulation of the inflammatory factor IL-8.
source: In addition, treatment of HCT-8 intestinal epithelial cells with 1 mM indole inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) mediated activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and up-regulation of the inflammatory factor IL-8, thus improving intestinal epithelial barrier function (Bansal et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Bansal et al., 2010).

claim: Indole limits the bacterial proliferation in the gut of worms by driving intestinal defense gene expression via DAF-16.
source: Our data show that indole limits the bacterial proliferation in the gut of worms by driving intestinal defense gene expression via DAF-16.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing indole activates DAF-16, which up-regulates lysozymes that reduce bacterial loads.

claim: The bacteria-derived metabolite may serve as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern that is recognized by metazoans.
source: These findings suggest that the bacteria-derived metabolite may serve as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern that is recognized by metazoans.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that indole from bacteria activates host defense responses.

claim: Indole at a higher concentration (5 mM) is capable of inhibiting cell division in E. coli K12 strain.
source: Although indole at a higher concentration (5 mM) is capable of inhibiting cell division in E. coli K12 strain (Chimerel et al., 2012), exogenous indole has little effect on the growth of E. coli K12 strain up to 3 mM (Chant and Summers, 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Chimerel et al., 2012).

claim: Exogenous indole has little effect on the growth of E. coli K12 strain up to 3 mM.
source: Although indole at a higher concentration (5 mM) is capable of inhibiting cell division in E. coli K12 strain (Chimerel et al., 2012), exogenous indole has little effect on the growth of E. coli K12 strain up to 3 mM (Chant and Summers, 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Chant and Summers, 2007).

claim: Extracellular indole concentrations detected in stationary phase LB cultures are typically 0.5–1 mM depending on the specific E. coli strain.
source: In general, extracellular indole concentrations detected in stationary phase LB cultures are typically 0.5–1 mM depending on the specific E. coli strain (Zarkan et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Zarkan et al., 2020).

claim: Indole is sufficient to inhibit the accumulation of E. coli BW25113 at the concentration range from 0.05 to 0.2 mM.
source: Our data show that indole is sufficient to inhibit the accumulation of E. coli BW25113 at the concentration range from 0.05 to 0.2 mM.
evidence: Stated based on experimental results showing reduced CFU with indole supplementation.

claim: Direct causal involvement of cell cycle arrest in E. coli by indole is unlikely.
source: Thus, these results suggest that direct causal involvement of cell cycle arrest in E. coli by indole is unlikely.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that effective indole concentrations are below those that directly inhibit bacterial growth.

claim: The cold-sensitive TRP channel TRPA-1 in neurons is involved in indole-mediated nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine.
source: Our data demonstrate that the cold-sensitive TRP channel TRPA-1 in neurons is involved in indole-mediated nuclear translocation of DAF-16 in the intestine, which is required for lifespan extension in C. elegans.
evidence: Demonstrated by tissue-specific RNAi experiments showing neuronal TRPA-1 is required.

claim: Both indole and indole-3-carboxaldehyde (IAld) are TRPA-1 agonists in vertebrates.
source: Recently, Ye et al., 2021 have shown that both indole and indole-3-carboxaldehyde (IAld) are TRPA-1 agonists in vertebrates.
evidence: Cited from recent study (Ye et al., 2021).

claim: trpa-1 is widely expressed in a variety of sensory neurons in worms.
source: trpa-1 is widely expressed in a variety of sensory neurons in worms (Kindt et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Kindt et al., 2007).

claim: Low temperature activates TRPA-1, which in turn acts to promote longevity via the PKC-2–SGK-1–DAF-16 pathway.
source: Low temperature also activates TRPA-1, which in turn acts to promote longevity via the PKC-2–SGK-1–DAF-16 pathway (Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Xiao et al., 2013).

claim: Unlike indole, activation of TPRA-1 by low temperature promotes the transcription activity, but not the nuclear translocation, of DAF-16.
source: It should be noted that unlike indole, activation of TPRA-1 by low temperature promotes the transcription activity, but not the nuclear translocation, of DAF-16 (Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Xiao et al., 2013) and contrasted with current findings.

claim: Knockdown of sgk-1 does not influence the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 induced by indole.
source: Furthermore, our data show that knockdown of sgk-1 dose not influence the nuclear translocation of DAF-16 induced by indole.
evidence: Shown by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Indole extends lifespan via TRPA-1 only in nervous system, whereas low temperature extends lifespan via TRPA-1 both in the intestine and neurons.
source: Finally, indole extends lifespan via TRPA-1 only in nervous system, whereas low temperature extends lifespan via TRPA-1 both in the intestine and neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by tissue-specific RNAi experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Indole-mediated lifespan extension is essentially different from low temperature-mediated lifespan extension, although TRPA-1 and DAF-16 are involved in both processes.
source: Thus, indole-mediated lifespan extension is essentially different from low temperature-mediated lifespan extension, although TRPA-1 and DAF-16 are involved in both processes.
evidence: Concluded from differences in tissue specificity and mechanism.

claim: Only neurons with activated TRPA-1 may release a neurotransmitter, which in turn triggers a signaling pathway to extend the lifespan of worms via activating DAF-16 in a non-cell autonomous manner.
source: One possibility is that only neurons with activated TRPA-1 may release a neurotransmitter, which in turn triggers a signaling pathway to extend the lifespan of worms via activating DAF-16 in a non-cell autonomous manner, while the intestinal activated TRPA-1 is unable to release the neurotransmitter.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis to explain tissue-specific effects.

claim: TRPA-1 induces the releasing of calcitonin gene-related peptide in perivascular sensory nerves, which in turn binds corresponding G-protein-coupled receptor, and causes membrane hyperpolarization and arterial dilation on smooth muscle cells.
source: Indeed, TRPA-1 induces the releasing of calcitonin gene-related peptide in perivascular sensory nerves, which in turn binds corresponding G-protein-coupled receptor, and causes membrane hyperpolarization and arterial dilation on smooth muscle cells (Talavera et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Talavera et al., 2020) to support the neurotransmitter hypothesis.

claim: DAF-16 inhibits bacterial proliferation by up-regulating expression of two lysozyme genes, lys-7 and lys-8.
source: In this study, our data demonstrate that DAF-16 inhibits bacterial proliferation by up-regulating expression of two lysozyme genes, lys-7 and lys-8.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression analysis and CFU measurements in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Lysozymes play an important role in the innate immunity in both vertebrate and invertebrate animals.
source: As a group of digestive enzymes with antimicrobial properties, lysozymes play an important role in the innate immunity in both vertebrate and invertebrate animals (O'Rourke et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous study (O'Rourke et al., 2006).

claim: lys-7 has been proven to play an important role in resistance against a variety of pathogens.
source: As a target gene of DAF-16, lys-7 has been proven to play an important role in resistance against a variety of pathogens, such as Microbacterium nematophilum (O'Rourke et al., 2006), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Nandakumar and Tan, 2008), the pathogenic E. coli LF82 (Simonsen et al., 2011), Bacillus thuringiensis (Boehnisch et al., 2011), and Cryptococcus neoformans (Marsh et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: A mutation in lys-7 significantly reduces the lifespan, but does not influence the accumulation of E. coli OP50 in the intestine of 2-day-old worms.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that a mutation in lys-7 significantly reduces the lifespan, but does not influence the accumulation of E. coli OP50 in the intestine of 2-day-old worms (Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Portal-Celhay et al., 2012).

claim: The lys-7 mutants exhibit reduced lifespan and elevated bacterial loads in the intestine of worms on days 4 and 7.
source: In the current study, the lys-7 mutants exhibit reduced the lifespan and elevated bacterial loads in the intestine of worms on days 4 and 7.
evidence: Stated based on experimental results in Figure 6.

claim: The lys-7;lys-8 double mutants exhibit a comparable accumulation of E. coli OP50 in worms on day 1.
source: Actually, our data also show that the lys-7;lys-8 double mutants exhibit a comparable accumulation of E. coli OP50 in worms on day 1.
evidence: Stated based on experimental results.

claim: lys-8 mutation does not influence either the lifespan or bacterial loads, but it enhances the effect of lys-7.
source: Although lys-8 mutation dose not influence either the lifespan or bacterial loads, it enhances the effect of lys-7.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes.

claim: lys-8 acts in synergy with lys-7 to limit bacterial accumulation in the gut of worms.
source: These results suggest that lys-8 acts in synergy with lys-7 to limit bacterial accumulation in the gut of worms.
